title.en: Types of solutions, hydrated salts and deliquescence
Why sea water is not just water

text.en: Sea water, the air we breathe and the blood in our body are all solutions. Knowing how solutions are made and classified helps us understand why blue copper sulphate crystals turn white on heating and why caustic soda pellets turn wet in open air.

A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances; the component present in the smaller amount is the solute and the one in the larger amount is the solvent.
A binary solution has one solute and one solvent, like copper sulphate in water, and a ternary solution has three components, like salt and sugar both dissolved in water.
Based on the physical states, solutions can be solid in solid, such as copper in gold, liquid in solid, such as mercury in sodium, solid in liquid, such as salt in water, liquid in liquid, such as alcohol in water, gas in liquid, such as soda water, and gas in gas, such as air.
Based on the solvent, an aqueous solution has water as solvent and is the commonest, because water is called the universal solvent.
A non-aqueous solution uses another solvent, such as sulphur in carbon disulphide or iodine in carbon tetrachloride.
All solutions are mixtures, but not all mixtures are solutions, because a solution must be uniform throughout.
When ionic substances crystallise from water, their ions attract water molecules which stay in the crystal in a fixed ratio; this is called hydration, and the number of water molecules is the water of crystallisation.
Blue vitriol, CuSO4.5H2O, has five water molecules; on gentle heating it loses them and becomes colourless anhydrous copper sulphate, and adding water brings the blue colour back.
Other hydrated salts are Epsom salt MgSO4.7H2O, gypsum CaSO4.2H2O, green vitriol FeSO4.7H2O and white vitriol ZnSO4.7H2O.
Hygroscopic substances absorb moisture from air without changing their state, like concentrated sulphuric acid, phosphorus pentoxide, quicklime and silica gel, so they are used as drying agents.
Deliquescent substances absorb so much moisture that they dissolve in it, like caustic soda, caustic potash and ferric chloride; deliquescence is greatest at low temperature and in humid air.
So hygroscopic substances stay in the same state after absorbing moisture, while deliquescent substances lose their crystal shape and form a saturated solution.

problem.en: Blue crystals turn white when heated and become blue again when a few drops of water are added. Explain, and name the substance.

text.en: The blue crystals are copper sulphate pentahydrate, CuSO4.5H2O, a hydrated salt with five molecules of water of crystallisation.

why.en: Blue colour comes from the hydrated form.

text.en: On heating it loses the five water molecules and becomes colourless anhydrous copper sulphate.

why.en: Heating removes the water of crystallisation.

text.en: Adding water or cooling makes it take the water back and turn blue again, so the change is reversible.

prompt.en: Describe the types of solutions and explain the difference between hygroscopic and deliquescent substances.

requiredIdeas.en: Hygroscopic absorb moisture, deliquescent dissolve in it

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking every mixture is a solution
Thinking hygroscopic substances dissolve in the moisture they take

points.en: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute in a solvent; solutions are binary or ternary.
Water is the universal solvent; sulphur dissolves in carbon disulphide, a non-aqueous solvent.
Hydrated salts have water of crystallisation, such as CuSO4.5H2O.
Hygroscopic substances absorb moisture; deliquescent substances absorb enough to dissolve.
